Armed Conflict & Security
• The US abruptly redeployed B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford amid a potential threat, while Downing Street insisted the UK base remains secure.
• Russia escalated drone strikes in Kyiv, reportedly targeting bridges, as the Ukraine front remains largely static and increasingly dominated by evolving drone warfare; civilians in occupied Oleshky face hunger and landmine dangers.
• Investigators say a Flydubai co-pilot intended to crash a plane into Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport, highlighting aviation security risks.
• Nigeria police say bombs are hindering efforts to rescue 19 abducted youths; separately, a mass shooting at a Georgia homecoming killed two and injured dozens, and a U.S. Marine’s arrest in Okinawa spurred protests.
Why it matters: Security threats from state and non-state actors are straining military postures, civilian safety, and critical infrastructure across multiple regions.

• Supporters of jailed former PM Imran Khan marched in Pakistan after talks with authorities collapsed, demanding his release and medical care.
• Spain’s PM Pedro Sánchez called a snap election for November 29 after defeats on housing measures amid nationwide protests.
• The UK Green Party’s vote to define Zionism as racism drew sharp condemnation, intensifying debates over antisemitism and free speech.
• Protests in Japan grew after a U.S. Marine’s arrest in a woman’s killing in Okinawa; separately, Channel crossings turned deadly as anti-migrant protests erupted in Gosport.
Why it matters: Rising civil unrest over governance, rights, and identity politics is testing institutions and policing, with implications for social cohesion and democratic processes.

Longevity & Anti-Aging
• Researchers built an aging clock from images of hematopoietic stem cell nuclei, leveraging structural DNA changes as biomarkers of biological age.
• A Nature Aging study linked age-related decline in chaperone-mediated autophagy to impaired macrophage clearance of senescent cells, suggesting autophagy restoration could reduce senescent burden.
• The antimicrobial K21 improved macrophage mitophagy and extended lifespan in nematodes, hinting at immune-metabolic routes to longevity.
• A review challenged myths about older adults’ mobility in cities, stressing the diversity of aging experiences and the risks of ageist policy.
Why it matters: New biomarkers and cellular quality-control insights are informing interventions to extend healthspan, while urban design and policy must adapt to an aging population.

Le Labo’s Concrete Home Diffuser Turns Scent Into Light
Entertainment.text: SummaryLe Labo reworks its home diffuser in hand-cast concrete, replacing earlier wooden housings.A nebulizer disperses SANTAL 26 while an Edison bulb responds to scent intensity.The limited edition launches October 5 ahead of a wider December rollout.Le Labo is giving its home fragrance ritual a more architectural edge with the Concrete Home Diffuser, a limited-edition reinterpretation of its previously wood-bodied diffusers. This special edition embraces a raw, industrial edge with a base made entirely of concrete. Cast, polished, and sealed by hand in the U.S., the material inherently features natural color variations and air voids that ensure no two pieces are exactly alike. Over time, the heavy concrete is designed to develop a unique patina, transforming the utilitarian home fragrance device into a distinctive, personalized heirloom.Beyond its sculptural appearance, the Concrete Home Diffuser utilizes proprietary technology to deliver an immersive sensory experience that merges both scent and light. Inside, an advanced nebulizer mechanism breaks down Le Labo's signature fragrance oils into an ultra-fine mist. This process meticulously preserves the full olfactive integrity of the scent without the need for heating or diluting the oil. Complementing the nebulizer is a vintage-inspired Edison bulb that intelligently syncs with the intensity of the scent diffusion, dimming and brightening in tandem with the fragrance output.The complete set includes the concrete diffuser base, SANTAL 26 Diffuser Oil, diffuser bulb, light bulb and a waxed canvas tote bag, with replacement fragrance oil and light bulbs also offered separately. The combination of concrete, glass and warm filament light places the diffuser somewhere between fragrance device, lighting object and collectible home accessory, extending Le Labo’s pared-back visual language beyond scent alone. The Concrete Home Diffuser launches in select markets on today, before receiving a wider global rollout starting December 1, 2026. For more information, visit Le Labo’s official website.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Moncler Re/Icons 2026 Reworks Four Archive Icons, From a 1954 K2 Parka to the '80s Tibb
Entertainment.text: SummaryMoncler Re/Icons 2026 rebuilds the Karakorum, Verone, Himalaya and Tibb in lighter, refined materials and tonal colorEvery jacket shares new archive-inspired details, including an interior label of Vittorio Sella's 1909 photograph of K2The season adds windbreakers, tees, pants, skirts and climbing goggle-inspired sunglasses, plus a book and a feature film tie-inMoncler Re/Icons returns for 2026 with four archive styles reworked for today: the Karakorum, Verone, Himalaya and Tibb. The pieces range from 1950s expedition gear to 1980s cult favorites. Built around the FW season theme "Pioneers in Moncler with Extraordinary Dreams," the collection pairs the brand's mountaineering roots with modern construction. It also pushes Re/Icons into full ready-to-wear looks for the first time.A set of shared details connects the four jackets. Each uses a camaïeu technique, layering several shades from the same color family for a rich, tonal finish. Inside, a label reproduces Vittorio Sella's photograph of K2, taken in June 1909. On the outside, metal logos fixed to the pockets borrow from the souvenir pins once collected in alpine towns.The Karakorum carries the deepest history. Moncler made it in 1954 for Achille Compagnoni and Lino Lacedelli, the members of the Italian expedition who completed the first ascent of K2, the second-highest mountain on Earth. The original was raw cotton filled with down. The 2026 version switches to a glossy 10-denier micro ripstop, cut in a rounded, enveloping shape that stays light. It keeps its practical features: a double snap-button front, a removable hood, a drawstring coulisse and internal shoulder straps that let it be carried like a backpack. A large chest pocket carries the updated Re/Icons logo. Men's colorways are black, red and petrol blue; women's are black and purple.The Verone moves from the mountains to the city. It arrived in the 1980s and became a signature piece for Milan's Paninari, a youth scene that gathered around the city's cafés and treated the puffer as essential everyday wear. The new version uses lightweight matte micro cotton in a relaxed fit, with a pullout hood and a zip closure behind a buttoned storm placket. Women's colorways are pastel pink, lilac and black, while men's are navy, gray and black.The Himalaya is the most recent of the four. The short down jacket debuted in 2009 and later evolved into the Moncler Maya. Its design traces back to the 1950s, when Moncler equipped French climber Lionel Terray for his first ascent of Makalu in the Himalayas. The 2026 update uses a soft matte cotton-nylon blend in a relaxed fit and keeps the drawstring hood and logo-patch sleeve pocket. Men can choose off-white, brown, navy or black, and women get the same options plus pastel pink.The Tibb vest completes the lineup. Introduced in the 1980s, the oversized gilet is now reversible and comes in either recycled matte Longue Saison or wool gabardine. It keeps its boudin quilting, a double-zip closure with heritage round pullers and a metallic chest logo. Men's colors are black, gray, white and caramel; women's are white, pale pink, caramel and black.Beyond the jackets, Re/Icons now covers head to toe. The new range includes windbreakers, T-shirts, pants and skirts, along with beanies, balaclavas and silk-twill foulards. Titanium-and-leather sunglasses based on vintage climbing goggles complete the accessories.The archive story also extends to print and film. Alpine Diary is a book written as the journal of an invented 1950s explorer. It pairs handwritten entries and black-and-white images of historic climbs with color photography of the new collection. Moncler's first feature film collaboration, Bianco, stars Alessandro Borghi as climber Walter Bonatti and recreates the Karakorum for its cast. Bonatti wore the jacket during his 1961 climb of the Central Pillar of Frêney on Mont Blanc, an expedition that ended in tragedy. Bianco arrives in theaters in January 2027.Moncler Re/Icons 2026 previews during Paris Fashion Week on October 5 and 6 at Il Rifugio, a private space inside Moncler's Champs-Élysées store. The collection pre-launches exclusively at the Champs-Élysées store on October 8. A pop-up at Isetan in Tokyo and a pre-launch at Moncler Fifth Avenue follow on October 14, ahead of a global release at select Moncler stores and online on October 15.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: grounds’ SS27 “An Invitation” Turns Footwear Into Otherworldly Objects
Entertainment.text: Summarygrounds SS27 explores the unknown through its “An Invitation” theme.POTTER and LONPIE exaggerate heels through hollow, sculptural mega-soles.MOOPIE, LOOPIE, SKYSCRAPER and BAT styles expand the collection’s surreal footwear language.What if an invitation arrived from a realm beyond our knowledge, asking what we would wear to meet the unknown? Presented at the Église Américaine de Paris, Mikio Sakabe’s Spring/Summer 2027 collection for grounds, titled "An Invitation," confronts an over-informed world with radical surrealism. Rejecting the mundane patterns of daily life, the Japanese footwear label transforms shoes into speculative artifacts — objects bridging ancient ritual objects, futuristic robotics, and alien architecture. The atmospheric backdrop of the American Church in Paris sharpened this otherworldly tension, presenting footwear as a sacred armor for an unwritten future.At the center of that world is POTTER, a new line that pushes the conventional high heel into far more sculptural territory. Inspired by the enduring visual language of Japanese dogū figures, the silhouette sharpens the toe while dramatically expanding the volume beneath the foot. Its one-piece hollow sole curves around open cavities at the front and rear, creating a smooth, glass-like appearance that makes the shoe seem almost blown rather than molded. Standing around 10 cm high, POTTER moves between refinement and distortion across several variations, including Little Star, All In One, Slash, Trotte and Rino. Each interprets the same bulbous foundation differently: from pointed, almost court-shoe uppers to strapped constructions, sporty lace-ups and extended sock-like forms.The collection becomes more extreme with LONPIE, an amplified evolution of the LOOPIE structure first introduced for SS26. Enlarged into a mega-sole heel and fused with the silhouette of traditional Japanese koppori footwear, the design sits somewhere between gothic platform dressing and the armored feet of a robot anime character. Its scale is intentionally excessive — approximately 14 cm at the front and 20 cm at the rear — yet the sole is completely hollow, turning what appears massively heavy into a construction built around empty space. Elsewhere, grounds expands several of its established lines, moving between LOOPIE Mary Janes and ankle-cuff sandals, MOOPIE sneakers and boots, SKYSCRAPER models, JEWELRY silhouettes, JOG VISION FLUX, MANUS and the more aggressive BAT series. The breadth keeps SS27 from resting on a single oversized gesture, instead showing how the brand’s swollen sole language can move from feminine pumps and sandals to technical sneakers, boots and more hybridized shapes.Nude pink, yellow, dark green, white, gray and black form the core palette, with clear and aurora-like soles, metallic finishes, cloudy translucencies and jolts of brighter color making many of the shoes appear suspended somewhere between organic matter and manufactured object. Soft pink POTTER heels can look almost porcelain-like, while darker green and black iterations take on a more industrial character; elsewhere, transparent cushioning, glossy surfaces and exaggerated cavities make even the collection’s more familiar sneakers feel slightly alien. The result is a collection that turns footwear into part costume, part artifact — a wardrobe for crossing the threshold described by its mysterious invitation, without ever quite revealing what waits on the other side.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Miu Miu and New Balance Rework the RC150 With Toe-Tied Laces
Entertainment.text: Name: Miu Miu x New Balance RC150SKU: TBCRelease Date: February 2027Entering its fifth year of collaborative partnership, Miu Miu and New Balance have reunited to debut a fresh reinterpretation of the RC150 racing sneaker, which recently previewed on the French fashion house's Spring/Summer 2027 runway in Paris.Originally launched by New Balance in the late 1990s, the RC150 was conceived as a high-performance road-racing shoe celebrated for its groundbreaking, ultra-lightweight 150-gram construction. Today, vintage iterations of the model are exceptionally rare and hard to find. In the hands of Miu Miu, the heritage runner has been playfully subverted and decontextualized, transforming the familiar athletic silhouette into an unexpected, high-fashion statement piece with an effortless attitude.The collaborative New Balance x Miu Miu RC150 is heavily deconstructed, featuring a malleable technical mesh upper that is disrupted by prominent contrast zigzag embroidery across its entirety. Ensuring agility and everyday comfort, the extremely lightweight upper is paired with a flexible UltraLight sole. Adding a touch of the collaboration's signature irreverence, the sneakers are finished with interchangeable laces that are loosely knotted at the toe through external loops, encouraging individual personalization.Drawing direct inspiration from the original shoe's late-1990s origins, the collection's color palette offers both soft, muted tones and bold, vibrant iterations — including a striking, highly visible blue and bright yellow makeup showcased during the runway presentation. Entertainment.title: Michael Jordan's Championship Ferrari 550 Maranello Fetches $2.7 Million USD
Entertainment.text: SummaryMichael Jordan's 1997 Ferrari 550 Maranello sold for a record-breaking $2.7 million at a Joopiter auctionThe massive final price points to a generational shift in the collector market for cultural memorabiliaThe legendary sports car was recovered after a decade-long search that traced an incomplete VIN from an internet forumThe modern collector market just witnessed a monumental transaction as Michael Jordan's 1997 Ferrari 550 Maranello officially sold for a record $2.7 million USD on September 30. Hosted by the auction establishment Joopiter, which was founded by Pharrell Williams, the high-profile sale effortlessly eclipsed its initial estimated block of $700,000 USD to $1,300,000 USD. This final price represents roughly ten times the current market value of typical 550 Maranellos, which normally trade hands between $200,000 USD and $300,000 USD. Today, a generational shift in the high-end market drives collectors to pay unprecedented premiums for memorabilia connected to iconic cultural figures. The sale demonstrates how provenance and celebrity association now rival mechanical rarity in determining the value of vintage supercars.The basketball icon originally obtained the front-engined Ferrari new in late May of 1997. Procured through Foreign Cars Italia in North Carolina, the grand tourer arrived dripping in classic Italian aesthetic cues. This vehicle is painted in Rosso Barchetta and features a tan leather interior alongside striking chrome Speedline wheels. Bearing the specific chassis number 108712, the highly coveted vehicle stands as a rare piece of automotive history, serving as just one of the 3,083 550 Maranellos ever built by the marque.During his storied ownership period, Jordan drove the car for around 6,400 miles, actively utilizing the machine for commutes to Chicago Bulls games and team practices. While Jordan owned the vehicle, it proudly wore an Illinois vanity plate that read "MJ 5". His sports car was heavily tied to his legendary championship run. Mere hours after winning his fifth NBA Championship on June 13, 1997, Jordan famously left the United Center sitting behind the wheel of the Ferrari. Its physical presence left a lasting cultural mark, as sneaker designer Tinker Hatfield directly referenced the car's shape when designing the Air Jordan XIV shoe.Jordan eventually sold the Ferrari in late 2002 via Lake Forest Sportscars in the Chicago area. The car was subsequently purchased by a California owner and did not emerge for public sale for 24 years. It was finally unearthed by John Temerian, founder of the supercar seller Curated, who located the vehicle following an exhaustive decade-long search. Temerian managed to track it down by recreating an incomplete VIN from an internet forum using Ferrari dealer records. Bringing its rich history full circle, the car traveled back to Chicago in May for a pre-sale photoshoot on the grounds of Jordan's mansion.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Lacoste Unveils Spring/Summer 2027 Collection at Paris Fashion Week
Entertainment.text: The Lacoste Spring/Summer 2027 runway show unfolded at the iconic Court Philippe-Chatrier. The set design paid homage to the raw beauty of earthy materials, their rich textures and tones, and the industrial machinery used to produce the famous clay courts. Inspired by this signature red clay, the entire show space was awash in rolling earth. The guest seating also nodded to the clay factories, while the runway itself—set across this demanding terrain—echoed the collection’s relentless exploration of speed.For the Spring/Summer 2027 collection, Lacoste Creative Director Pelagia Kolotouros introduces a new creative vision: tennis apparel is no longer bound by traditional uniforms, but serves as a canvas for individual expression. This ethos defines the season's core theme—Dress Code: Beyond White.Kolotouros envisions the court as a space in constant flux. Footwork overlaps, lines blur; clay dusts the hems of skirts, and sweat becomes a badge of honor. Traces once deemed imperfections are now celebrated as testaments to achievement, forming the foundation of this season’s design language. Spotless white uniforms make way for garments that bear the vibrant marks of intense athletic exertion. The clothes move with the body rather than restricting it: tailoring skims the silhouette without compromising movement. In the focused moment before a serve, every detail matters—from the drape of the fabric and the painted lines of the court to the steady rhythm of a breath.This season shatters the rigid constraints and hierarchies of traditional preppy style. Cottons are garment-dyed and enzyme-washed to soften stiff structures and release a fluid, effortless energy. Tropical wools are deconstructed for a relaxed, supple feel, while washed silks retain their raw, natural texture, stripping away any formal stuffiness. Fine jersey knits feature delicate perforations to enhance breathability and freedom of movement, and technical fabrics are finished with rolled hems to cultivate an effortlessly relaxed attitude.On the runway, deep teal coats and softly tailored suits were styled in relaxed, belted silhouettes, accented with lanyards and neon yellow charms. Oversized piqué polo shirts were layered over technical long-sleeve knits and paired with semi-pleated skirts. Bright cobalt nylon tracksuits and vibrant orange zip-up vests channeled the dynamic energy of a pre-match warm-up. White jackets and wide-leg trousers featured hems artfully dusted with faux red clay, resembling authentic stains from the court. Crinkled cottons and graphic tees completed a versatile wardrobe designed for endless, personalized mixing and matching.Two standout accessories brought the spirit of the court to the streets. Echoing the graphic tees and lanyards, the new René bag drew inspiration from Irving Penn’s iconic 1984 photograph of a polo shirt. Featuring an asymmetric flap that mimics the casual drape of a cotton piqué collar, the bag is available in pure white, an ombré clay hue, and mirrored silver. The sculptural ACE-T1 cage sneaker pays homage to the taut tension of a tennis net, capturing the essence of power and speed in three variations: a casual sneaker, a tennis wedge, and a lace-up pump.The season’s color palette is drawn straight from the post-match terrain, grounded in sun-baked clay and mineral earth tones. Pops of metallic silver, neon yellow, and cobalt blue punctuate the collection, delivering a vibrant jolt of visual tension.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Art & Culture.title: Theaster Gates Buys America’s Last Luxury Porcelain Maker
Art & Culture.text: SummaryGates acquired Pickard China, the last remaining U.S. maker of high-end porcelain.He plans to guide the company’s creative future while expanding his own ceramics practice into porcelain.Chicago-based artist Theaster Gates has acquired Pickard China, the last remaining high-end porcelain manufacturer in the U.S.Founded in 1893 and based in Antioch, Illinois, Pickard has spent more than a century producing porcelain for clients ranging from the White House and U.S. embassies to hotels, private clubs and major retailers. In recent decades, however, the company has faced slower production and an aging factory in need of major upgrades.Gates first connected with Pickard while searching for an American manufacturer for a homewares project with Prada. Andy Pickard Morgan, the fourth-generation family member who has led the company since 2006, later approached Gates about taking over the business as he prepared for retirement and no one in the family planned to continue running it.The acquisition feels like a natural extension of Gates’ wider practice. Ceramics have been central to his work for years, drawing from both Japanese and African American traditions while also bringing attention to overlooked figures in ceramic history. Outside the studio, Gates has become known for restoring buildings and giving new life to cultural spaces and archives across Chicago’s South Side.Speaking to NPR about Pickard’s future, Gates said the idea of the company “bringing artisanal manufacturing back to the fore” was especially exciting.Gates will lead Pickard’s creative direction while putting together a management team to oversee its daily operations. Pickard Morgan will remain involved in an executive role. The artist also sees the factory as a chance to expand his own work with ceramics into porcelain, bringing his artistic practice directly into the future of the historic American manufacturer.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Art & Culture.title: Ma Yansong Reads the Salomon XT-RIDGE Like a Building
Art & Culture.text: Why would a sneaker catch an architect's eye?As a new silhouette branching off the XT family, the XT-RIDGE carries Salomon's mountain DNA while taking a sharp turn in design. It sets aside the exposed SensiFit™ cage that has long defined the XT line's visual language, drawing instead on the layered light and shadow of modern architecture. Using semi-translucent TPU, it reworks the idea of a ridgeline with a more restrained hand, translating performance know-how from the mountains into the context of the urban climb."Seeing comes before words," wrote British art critic John Berger in Ways of Seeing, arguing that the way we look at anything is shaped by our own experience, culture and knowledge.Outdoor culture is increasingly bleeding into city life, and the performance vocabulary of materials, structure and function has found its way into architecture, design and fashion. With the XT-RIDGE, this act of seeing becomes especially interesting. Once the signature exposed framework is pulled back and stripped away, the interplay of visible and hidden structure, along with a clean, restrained geometric profile, gives the shoe an order that recalls a modern building facade. Complex support systems are tucked beneath the surface, while solid and void, open and closed, create layers across different materials. The result gives technical structures built for mountain sport a more contemporary aesthetic expression.The same shoe means different things to different people. An everyday consumer might first notice its colorway, style and brand. An athlete pays attention to support, grip and performance. For an architect who works with space and structure, a shoe invites another way of seeing: how materials organize a surface, how structure establishes order, and how the moving body fits within that micro-scale system.Because the XT-RIDGE takes its cues from architectural structure and layered light, Salomon partnered with internationally renowned architect Ma Yansong for an architect's reading of the shoe. Following his gaze, from mountain experience to structural relationships and architectural aesthetics, we look closer at a shoe that is understated on the outside and considered within.How a Shoe Becomes Architecture at Its Smallest ScaleTo understand how an architect sees a shoe, you first have to move your eye from its overall silhouette to its internal structure.Ma noted in our conversation that while a shoe is far smaller than a building, both relate directly to the human body. Both need a complete design logic built on form, structure, function and the relationship between inside and outside.Seen this way, the XT-RIDGE is architecture at its smallest scale. The layered upper interweaves different materials to create a surface with depth. The technical mesh sits between open and closed, mediating breathability, lockdown and visual layering. Supportive overlays then step into the structure, providing stability while tracing the shoe's geometric outline. Each element serves its own function, yet none stands alone; through layering, covering and connecting, they form a unified whole.This logic shares common ground with the way architecture handles material and space. A building cannot stand on its skin alone. Its final form depends on structure and support, the less visible but more essential parts. In the same way, the XT-RIDGE folds support, protection and breathability directly into its outer form. When an architect looks at it, what he sees is how different structures beneath the upper work together to form a harmonious whole.Bringing Landscape Into the CityThe dense grid of urban life tends to produce a narrow, limited sensory experience. Steel and concrete build a modern order, but they also quietly compress our imagination. By contrast, the unpolished rocks, rolling mountains and moving water of natural landscapes open up a vast inner world through sheer primal force.Ma's architectural practice has long tried to break through this flattening of perception in the city.He has consistently brought nature into urban settings, creating buildings that breathe. At the newly completed Shenzhen Bay Culture Park, he shaped a massive complex into what reads as a cluster of seaside boulders, set in striking contrast and dialogue with the dense skyline around it. At Quzhou Sports Campus, he turned conventional stadiums into rolling, earth-covered green hills, growing a volcano-like natural cluster out of the city's dense fabric. These projects carry the expansive imagery of mountains and water into the city, quietly rebuilding the emotional connection between people and nature.This approach resonates deeply with THE RIDGE STATE, the idea behind the Salomon XT-RIDGE. Here, the ridge goes beyond a single landform in nature and becomes a transitional zone linking mountain trails to the edges of the city.As a vessel connecting different spaces, the XT-RIDGE carries Salomon's long memory of the mountains. It translates the balance, support and protection needed on complex terrain into a design language suited to the pace of contemporary city life. Whether the wearer moves across fair-faced concrete, crowded streets or the urban fringe, the shoe still awakens that intuitive dialogue between body and terrain. The boundary between mountain and city dissolves through continuous movement.Silent Ascent: Arriving, and Still Moving ForwardOver a long enough timeline, whether in Salomon's enduring mountain heritage or Ma's own winding creative path, real strength often lies in quietly continuing forward.That spirit has shaped Salomon's trajectory from the start. Founded in the French Alps in 1947, the brand began with ski bindings and went on to explore skiing, mountaineering, trail running and other mountain sports, continually turning performance, innovation and its understanding of the mountains into new gear. Today, this forms the foundation of the XT-RIDGE's "silent ascent." Climbing here is less about the act of summiting and more a continuous, steady and quiet state of progress: still moving forward after you arrive.For Ma, this mirrors his own creative mindset. He doesn't see arrival as a fixed endpoint. Instead, he likens the different stages of his practice to layered mountain ranges, with rises and falls, where the undulating process itself holds immense value.On the XT-RIDGE, the silent ascent takes the form of steady, sustained movement. The shoe carries Salomon's accumulated mountain experience, bringing the balance, judgment and endurance developed on difficult terrain into everyday city life. The smooth extension of the ridge becomes a way for the wearer to move through the urban environment: every step changes, yet every step keeps its own pace and rhythm.So when a shoe carrying this mountain memory lands in an architect's field of vision as a "micro-building," what kind of reading does it receive?Following the ridgeline from the mountains into the city, Hypebeast sat down with Ma Yansong for an in-depth conversation. Starting from the mechanics of a shoe, he talks about the relationship between nature, architecture and the city, and how he keeps moving forward through a long, undulating career on his own silent ascent.This interview was conducted in Putonghua and has been translated and edited for length and clarity. Hypebeast: Some say "the shoe is the smallest scale of architecture." What do you make of that idea?Ma Yansong: A shoe is small, really small compared to a building, but both relate to people. Both need a shape and a structure. Architecture is the same in terms of inside and outside. The way its function, structure and space are reflected on the exterior follows a very tight logic.You wore the XT-RIDGE for today's shoot. How did it feel, and what stood out to you?It's really comfortable, the kind of shoe you don't want to take off once it's on. Actually, I've recently become interested in the question of how architecture can make people feel comfortable. I used to find function quite challenging. What exactly is the most comfortable state? I once had a theory that spiritual fulfillment might matter more than pure physical comfort. If everything is too comfortable, people can become lazy and lose some room for imagination.For example, when you face a building, you might think, "Why does it look a bit strange?" But as you try to understand it, you find the design has its own logic. You might not accept it at first glance, but as you keep experiencing and using it, you slowly realize why it was designed that way. I find that feeling, somewhere between unfamiliarity and understanding, really interesting.So I think the process of understanding the world comes through designing the things around us: a piece of furniture, a pair of shoes, a garment, an architectural space. Every design presents a way of seeing the world. Architecture is a lot like a shoe in that sense. In the end it's made for people to use, and it has aesthetics, structure and materials. Most of us only judge a material by whether it looks good, without knowing what's behind it. With a shoe, we don't really understand which materials are too breathable. With a building, it's insulation: how a space can be bright, energy-efficient and comfortable all at once is a highly scientific, specialized matter. The feeling it ultimately gives people is a crucial part of design.If you were to design a shoe for Salomon, what would it look like?If I designed a shoe, it would probably be quite abstract. Abstract things can feel a little unfamiliar at first, but they also seem to adapt better to different environments. You wear shoes to go to different places, into the mountains and rivers, into nature. How do you fit in with that environment? Function is important, of course, but I'd lean toward something abstract with a futuristic feeling.What is the relationship between "nature" and "the city" to you?I think they long for each other. In the city we all yearn for nature, because nature is so rare there. I grew up in old Beijing, where Shichahai, Jingshan and Beihai place nature inside the city. It's not only mountains and water, but also a certain mood: light, reflections, those beautiful things. Cities need nature, and nature also needs a human touch. Sometimes a traditional landscape painting includes a small bridge or a pavilion, and you see a person in that pavilion admiring the scenery. So when we talk about nature, there has to be a sense of human participation, of how people experience it.How do you see the relationship between architecture and nature, and how does it affect people?Cities are still too simple. The way people experience them is too uniform, and they lack enough room for imagination. Natural landforms let you imagine so many things. You see a few rocks and you might think of a universe, a planet, an island. These things can open up a huge inner world.Many fashion designers have a background in architecture. Where do you see the connection between the two?I think you can do anything after studying architecture. Some people lean toward rational thinking, method and logic. Others lean toward the emotional, more artistic and free-spirited. Combining the two is architecture. People trained in architecture also understand what kinds of trouble and resistance you'll run into when taking a dream from imagination to reality. You don't get scared off by those difficulties. You realize it step by step.In your daily life, what moment feels most like "moving forward even after you've arrived?"I don't feel there's any moment where I have to stop. The overall line is what matters. It's a bit like layers of mountain ranges. I work on different projects back and forth, and each work has its own rises and falls for me. I'm not after a steady line; I really pursue that undulation. You explore, and you don't know what's beyond the line. I value continuity, but that continuity needs a lot of new energy for me to feel excited. It's not about repeating the same thing. So the line stays fairly unknown and full of movement.If you placed the XT-RIDGE in a space as a piece of architecture, would you choose the city or nature?Definitely the city. What I've always done is bring nature into the city. Take the stadium project I did in Zhejiang, Quzhou Sports Campus. It looks like a cluster of volcanoes covered in rolling green slopes, a very surreal landscape. Placing nature into a city built on a grid feels completely different. I think we still need to return to nature, to get close to it and experience it. When the human spirit is placed in that kind of environment, it becomes very free, and you can imagine many interesting things.Architecture demands a long commitment, and buildings exist across long spans of time. How do you think about continuity?When I talk about being "constant," I don't mean repeating the same thing. First of all, I don't like repetition. I always hope to find something new. At the same time, our work places a lot of weight on criticality: first recognizing what problems exist in reality. Living in a city, which places make you uncomfortable, which buildings or spaces have problems, what do you want to change? Design often starts from that critical point. So each time you have a new goal, something new you want to change. That's what I've always done. I keep changing, but my working method is consistent, because I keep challenging and keep questioning.Where do you usually draw inspiration for your architecture?Anything emotional: stories, films, music, literature, anything that resonates with people. I've been thinking about this lately. Some mediums move people more easily. Reading a book or watching a film can change a lot of our ideas, but architecture seems slower. When we look at a building, we first ask how functional it is, or we judge whether it looks good. Its emotional connection with people doesn't seem as obvious as with other mediums.Architecture brings so many things together. So many film stories and spatial emotions take place within architecture. So I'm also thinking about how architecture can have a closer relationship with people's emotions and feelings.Both your work and the Salomon XT-RIDGE try to merge tradition, the future and the present. How can history be properly translated into the future?We are history. To the people who come after us, we are history. History is also a line, like a river that never stops. As Confucius said of the river, time keeps flowing past. So we should think about how future generations will see us, and also recognize that we, like those before us on this line, are an equal and natural part of it. There's no need to over-emphasize it. Even without so-called predecessors, we ourselves are history; we're already part of that line.Take what I said about old Beijing's influence on me. What I saw growing up, what I experienced and felt, the culture I was exposed to, all of it shaped me subtly. When you understand or express something, those values are already there invisibly, so there's no need to deliberately display tradition.I love the future and have always pursued futuristic things. Sometimes people sense an Eastern quality in my work, while others think it looks nothing like traditional architecture. But I care more about an inner connection than surface form. I'm not consciously trying to create a "future East" or a "future tradition," but those things may naturally exist in my work. Something truly new might be something neither the East nor the West has seen before, but it always has a source. It can't just leap out of a stone.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Art & Culture.title: Wonderwall® Designs a Forest Retreat for NOT A HOTEL KITAKARUIZAWA
Art & Culture.text: SummaryWonderwall®︎-designed villa MASU opens at NOT A HOTEL KITAKARUIZAWA.Based on a 4x4-meter grid, the design reimagines traditional Sukiya architecture.Interiors seamlessly blend custom designs, modern art, and iconic mid-century furniture.NOT A HOTEL KITAKARUIZAWA has unveiled MASU, a new forest retreat designed by Masamichi Katayama-led Wonderwall®, where the restraint of Japanese architecture meets the clarity of mid-century modernism.Built around the concept “Suki ni sumu" (As you like it), the project takes inspiration from architect Kenzo Tange’s 1953 residence in Seijo, reinterpreting its dialogue between traditional Japanese spatial thinking and modernist structure for contemporary living. At its core is a modular system of eight 4 x 4-meter “masu” on the upper floor, framed by a steel structure and a continuous 360-degree deck that dissolves the boundary between the home and North Karuizawa’s surrounding woodland. Below, a pilotis opens the dining area toward an outdoor living space and fire pit, while a light cantilevered staircase cuts through the double-height atrium, allowing daylight and air to move freely between levels.Inside, Wonderwall® approaches the residence less as a uniform interior than as a carefully assembled conversation between East and West, vintage and contemporary. Warm timber ceilings, expanses of glass and restrained architectural surfaces are offset by richly tactile elements, including custom furnishings designed specifically for MASU and a selection of mid-century classics.Isamu Noguchi’s sculptural Akari lighting illuminates the atrium, while pieces including George Nakashima’s CN108 Bench, Eero Saarinen’s Womb Chair and stools by Jean Touret appear throughout. Mika Tajima’s Negative Entropy, which translates sound data into jacquard-woven imagery, adds another layer to the living area, while deep carpeting and low-slung seating give the otherwise disciplined geometry a softer, almost sunken lounge-like character. The result is deliberately composed without feeling overly pristine, balancing the precision of the architecture with the comfort and individuality associated with the Japanese notion of suki.That relationship with the landscape becomes most pronounced in MASU’s more private spaces. Floor-to-ceiling windows make the bedrooms feel suspended among the trees, while one entire 4 x 4-meter module is devoted to a bathroom equipped with a natural hot-spring bath and cold plunge, connected directly to an adjoining sauna and the wraparound deck for open-air cooling.Outdoors, a fireplace-centered living area is intentionally left open-ended for dining, reading or gathering around the fire, while each of the four houses incorporates its own distinctive additional “masu,” configured variously as a tea room, Japanese-style room, study, theater or bedroom. Spanning over 526 square meters of combined indoor and outdoor space, MASU officially open for booking through NOT A HOTEL KITAKARUIZAWA.NOT A HOTEL KITAKARUIZAWATsumagoi Village, Agatsuma District,Gunma Prefecture, Japan View this post on Instagram A post shared by NOT A HOTEL (@notahotel_official)Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast
